A Movement grant to Women Enabled International built on its previous work that was funded by CMI to use its research and report on disability justice to build evidence for advocacy. The report contributed to evidence-based advocacy centered on grassroots activists. WEI partnered with 11 other organizations to present and advocate in two global spaces, CSW and AWID, where donors and governments were present. Indicator 1.2. UAF FA supported one (1) WRO, Women Enabled International (WEI), a disability rights advocacy organization, to conduct philanthropic advocacy for improving the quality and quantity of resourcing of groups working at the intersection of gender and disability justice. Funding supported the planning and implementation of two advocacy events and a final report on a disability justice landscape mapping. The report informed the planning of two global advocacy events, including 1) a closed briefing, panel and lunch at CSW68, and 2) a session at the AWID, "Rising Together" conference, to draw attention to the increasd need for resourcing DJ movements from the perspectives of activists from the Middle East (West Asia) and Eastern Europe. Funds supported event logistics, access infrastructure and administrative fees to implement the events where funders and gender justice actors will come together in New York (CSW) and Thailand (AWID). Funds will also support the implementation of a Disability Justice Landscape Mapping report. Indicator 1.4. UAF FA's grant support for movement-building to WEI (Women Enabled International) engaged with 11 official partners who were part of planning and presentation at donor and civil society spaces to increase resourcing for disability justice at the intersection of gender. Eight (8) official partners planned and facilitated a closed donor briefing at CSW and three (3) partners co-presented and facilitated a panel session and group-breakouts at the AWID conference. Through the engagement and advocacy in these two spaces, these 11 partners strengthened their solidarity and unified political analysis on the intersections of disability justice and gender that enhanced their shared messaging to advocate for increased resourcing for DJ and gender.

Three grants made to movements in Lebanon in the West Asia region increased the organizations' capacities to raise awareness and deepen understanding around queerness, transness, disability rights and community mutual aid. These topics are not mainstream and very little public information has been researched, written or publicized in the region as well as in Arabic languages. Through these grants, the group's have strengthened their advocacy capacities through the use of articles shared on social media and online as forms of advocacy. 1) Through a grant to Jeem, a feminist news media, allowed for them to add important articles to its repository on unique topics of transness, disability and community/mutual aid that have not been covered previously in the region. These articles can be used by different communities and organizations in trying to advocate for trans and disability rights as well for mutual aid for the queer community. They collaborated with new partners - Qorras and Queer Mutual Aid - on developing the articles and ultimately publish them on Jeem’s website to reach a regional audience. The articles added to Jeem’s repository of knowledge in Arabic providing clear distinctive analysis on topics related to transness, disability and community/ mutual aid. The project was able to produce knowledge about topics in Arabic that have not been covered in addition to the repository of knowledge for the Arabic-speaking region. 2) A grant to a queer-led group in Lebanon highlighted in a written and published article titled, "Learning from Transness and Disability: Toward a Framework of Bodily Autonomy", how transness and disability contribute to shaping a person’s access to public life, in order to highlight cross-cutting issues faced by trans people and people with disabilities. It discussed how transness and disability through the framework of bodily autonomy and self-determination allows one to better appreciate the commonalities and intersections of these experiences, which is crucial for mobilizing, organizing, funding, and advocating for trans rights, disability rights, and bodily autonomy in all its forms. 3) A movement grant to Queer Mutual Aid in Lebanon also produced an article titled: "Queer Mutual Aid Lebanon: Centering the Marginalized". This essay focuses on two main things: a) an overview of Mutual Aid as a practice from the perspective of the ‘periphery’, from Lebanon AND from the queer community and b) demonstrates the potential economic, social, and political value that Mutual Aid can provide for communities struggling for freedom, dignity, and liberation. This paper not only provides a unique account of a vital form of organizing but also serves as a model to advocate, emulate or critique other grassroots organizers and organizations around the globe. Both of the pieces are circulated in Arabic and English.

In the context of an economic crisis and lack of recognition of bodily autonomy and self-determination that are linked to GBV and discrimination, two LGBTQI+ organizations in Lebanon co-wrote the articles in Arabic with their members, and collaborated with a feminist think-tank (Jeem). Jeem, in partnership with the two grantees, co-edited the two articles, translated into English, and disseminated on their website/platform for a wider audience reach to equip them with new perspectives that are from the populations impacted in order to shift their support for LGBTQI+ and the disability communities’ rights. Three grantees in Lebanon collaborated and co-published articles to address the lack of public discourse around disability, queerness, transness, as well as the gaps and unsustainability of existing policies, services and programs that exclude these communities (and are not driven by these communities) during the economic crisis across the country. The two articles, “Queer Mutual Aid Lebanon: Centering the Peripherized,” and “Learning from Transness and Disability: Toward a Framework of Bodily Autonomy,” highlighted the importance of centering these excluded communities and focused on intersections of these issues to address specific needs of these marginalized communities. The articles argue for replicating and advocating for more self-determined, community-led solutions such as community mutual aid/assistance to ensure more sustainable and community-appropriate solutions and services. In the context of a country-wide financial crisis where government and public programs fail these communities, these two articles have been publicized on Jeem’s website (a feminist think-tank) with the aim of disseminating and creating an opportunity to raise awareness, increase understanding and shift public and policymakers’ attitudes, policies, allocation of resources, and to create community programs and services that better serve and the reflect these communities’ needs.

The region that UAF FA supports the majority of movement grants in is West Asia (Lebanon, Iraq, Palestine and Jordan) where authoritarian governments coupled with political, economic crises and war/conflict are ongoing in the past three years. Given the upheavals in the region, law and order have been enforced under the guise of national security using authoritarianism and militarization measures that curtail basic civil and political rights, as well as restricts civic space. Within conflict situations, extremist religious factions have hampered women’s and LGBTQI+ rights, including GBV/DV both in the private and public sphere. WHRDs and non-binary defenders have been targeted in their families, communities by state and non-state actors. Thus, this context makes it very dangerous, risky and challenging to continue activism and engage in public advocacy and lobbying. For WROs and WHRDs who continue to engage in advocacy and lobbying, it will take some time to see change as they fight regressive laws, policies, practices and governance in hostile environments. We may have more information reported from grantees later this year about the three movement grants’ longer-term outcomes on articles that they recently published.
